title: Power from the Atom: Is Thorium the Answer?

pages.text: The lights go off, and the whole street groans. A few minutes later they come back, and nobody asks where the electricity came from. In Ghana, much of it comes from falling water at the Akosombo, Kpong, and Bui dams. Much of the rest comes from thermal power stations that burn natural gas or oil, and a growing share comes from solar panels. Water and sunlight are renewable sources of energy: nature replaces them. Gas and oil are non-renewable: once burnt, they are gone, and burning them releases carbon dioxide, which warms the planet.

pages.alt: A Ghanaian street at dusk with lights coming on, and three small inset pictures of a dam, a gas power station, and a field of solar panels.

pages.text: There is another source of energy, inside the atom itself. Every atom has a tiny centre called a nucleus. The nuclei of a few heavy elements, such as uranium, can be split in two. This is nuclear fission. Each split releases heat and sets off more splits, in a chain reaction. A nuclear power station controls this reaction inside a reactor. The heat boils water into steam, the steam spins a turbine, and the turbine drives a generator. The fuel is astonishingly concentrated. A pellet of uranium fuel the size of a fingertip releases about as much energy as a tonne of coal.

pages.text: A nuclear power station releases almost no carbon dioxide while it runs, and it works day and night, in any weather. But it has serious costs. The used fuel is radioactive. It gives out harmful radiation and must be stored safely for thousands of years. Accidents are rare, but when cooling fails, a reactor can overheat and melt. That happened at Chernobyl in 1986 and at Fukushima in 2011, and large areas had to be abandoned. Nuclear stations are also very expensive and slow to build, and uranium, like oil, is non-renewable.

pages.text: Thorium is a silvery, slightly radioactive metal, about three times as common in the Earth’s crust as uranium. On its own it cannot keep a chain reaction going. But inside a reactor it can absorb particles called neutrons and slowly change into a kind of uranium that can. One design dissolves the fuel in hot liquid salt instead of using solid rods. Because the salt is not under high pressure, the reactor cannot burst like an overheated boiler. If it gets too hot, the salt can be drained into a tank, where it cools and hardens. American scientists ran a small reactor of this kind in the 1960s.

pages.text: The idea was set aside for fifty years. Then China built a small experimental thorium reactor in the Gobi Desert. It started up in 2023, and in November 2025 its scientists announced that it had turned thorium into uranium fuel while running, the first time this had been done in a reactor of this kind. But it is tiny. It produces about 2 megawatts of heat, hundreds of times less than Akosombo’s output. Hot salt corrodes metal pipes. The reactor still produces radioactive waste, though less of the longest-lasting kind. Thorium is promising, but it is not yet a proven way to light a city.

pages.text: Ghana already has experience with atoms. A small research reactor has operated at Kwabenya, near Accra, since 1994. It is used for research and training, not for electricity. The country is now planning its first nuclear power station, with Nsuban in the Western Region as the preferred site. Is that wise? Scientists do not ask whether an energy source is perfect, because none is. They compare. How much does it cost? Is it safe? What waste does it leave? Does it work at night and in the dry season? Does it warm the climate? Good decisions come from honest comparisons.

activities.question: Which of these is a renewable source of energy?
What is nuclear fission?
options: The splitting of a heavy nucleus, which releases heat
The burning of uranium in air
The melting of metal in a furnace

activities.question: Why must used nuclear fuel be stored with great care?
options: It is radioactive and stays harmful for thousands of years
It can be burnt again like charcoal

activities.question: Apply it: A district must choose between a solar farm and a gas power station. Which question is the most scientific one to ask first?
options: Which one do other countries prefer?
How do they compare in cost, reliability, safety, waste, and climate?

activities.prompt: Arrange the energy changes in a nuclear power station.
items: Nuclei split in the reactor and release heat.
The heat boils water into steam.
The generator produces electricity for homes and factories.

glossary.definition: Describing an energy source that nature replaces, such as sunlight or falling water.
Describing an energy source that is used up, such as gas, oil, or uranium.
The tiny centre of an atom.
Nuclear fission: the splitting of a heavy nucleus, releasing heat.
Chain reaction: a reaction in which each step sets off the next.
